Andrew: So I usually try to escape the city at least once a weekend - it's my much-needed break!
Audrey: Nice! I Bet it's great to get away like that.
Andrew: Yep! Nature is so therapeutic for me. It's hard to put into words how great it feels to be surrounded by greenery or standing on top of a mountain breathing in the fresh air. So peaceful and invigorating.


Audrey: Wow, that view looks great! It really captures that calming and peaceful feeling. It must be really satisfying to capture that tranquility.
Andrew: Yeah! I try to capture those special moments and share that feeling with others.
Audrey: That's really cool! Spreading that peaceful feeling to others is such a great way to bring happiness and motivation.
Andrew: I agree! It brings me joy to spread that feeling and motivate people to find their own peace - it's like a ripple effect, spreading positivity.
Audrey: Absolutely. Not only the receiving end feels great, the person spreading it will feel great as well!
Andrew: Yeah, it's crazy how that can bring such great joy and calm to people.
Audrey: Yeah, by sharing something can make a big difference to others.
Andrew: Yup! We don't realize it, but even the littlest gestures can have a big effect. Spreading good vibes and joy, that's the goal right? So what's up? Anything new or fun going on?
Audrey: Not much has changed since we last talked. I'm busy taking care of my pets and spending time with them. It's really fulfilling.
Andrew: I bet it's awesome hanging out with them - do your dogs enjoy going on hikes?
Audrey: My dogs go nuts when we go on hikes! They love exploring new scents and being in nature - it's their happy place. I can tell by their wagging tails and expressions how much they love it. It's so great to see them having so much fun!
Andrew: Wow, that's great! I was wondering if you have any tips or tricks for keeping dogs safe when they're out and about?
Audrey: Definitely! Safety is super important for me. I even got them something special. They sure look funny, but it works!
Andrew: Awesome to see that you take such good care of your dogs! What else do you do when you walk them?
Audrey: When I take them out, we usually play fetch with a ball or frisbee. They love chasing it! We also meet other dog owners in the park and have a doggie playdate. It's a great way for me to chat with people and for them to make new friends.
Andrew: Wow, looks like fun! They sure look excited about playing fetch!
Audrey: They absolutely adore it! They have tons of energy and love meeting new pals at playdates. Plus, they always get excited when I bring those out.
Andrew: Aww, that's so cute! Do they enjoy wearing the party hats? And where did you find their playdates?
Audrey: The hats don't bother them, they just put them on for fun and treats. And the dog park is great place to start! They can run and mingle with other pooches. It's such a fun spot for playdates!
Andrew: That sounds great! Where is it located?
Audrey: It's right by the park we usually walk. It's a great spot with lots of trees and benches for us to watch the dogs play.
Andrew: That's awesome, not too far away then! I'll have to check it out. Thanks for the suggestion!
Audrey: Yup! Not at all! Let me know how it goes.
Andrew: Sure, I'll let you know. Always great chatting with you! Ttyl.

selected.name: Extract Comfort and Joy Sources
selected.description: Use when a message states that something cheers the user up, brings joy, or provides comfort.
content: During extraction, if the user mentions a pet, hobby, person, item, or activity that provides cheer, comfort, or emotional support, create a separate durable memory (preference, relationship, or state) capturing that source, even when the message also contains stress or negative events.
Do not merge the supportive source only into a negative-event candidate; it should be its own candidate so it survives later SKIP/MERGE decisions.
Extract only sources explicitly stated as supportive; do not infer unmentioned ones.
selected.rerank_reason: The conversation discusses activities and experiences that provide comfort, joy, and emotional support, such as hiking, spending time with pets, and sharing positive feelings. These elements meet the criteria for extracting comfort and joy sources.

nearby_not_selected.name: Extract Origin Events as Distinct Memories
nearby_not_selected.description: When a user explains how they started or got into an activity, hobby, or interest, including who introduced it or when it began.
content: During extraction, if a message contains an origin narrative (how the person started an activity, who introduced it, what prompted it, or a concrete start time), create a separate event memory for the origin in addition to any preference or state memory.
Record the causal source (person or circumstance) and the start time/age if stated; do not fold the origin into a generic preference summary.
If the origin names another person, also consider a relationship memory capturing that connection.
Emit at most one origin memory per activity per message; skip if the same origin is repeated later.

nearby_not_selected.name: Propagate Established Location to New Event Memories
nearby_not_selected.description: Use when extracting an event that lacks an explicit place, but earlier session messages establish a location.
content: Before finalizing an event candidate without an explicit location, scan earlier messages for a location where the speaker is currently staying or visiting.
If the event's timing overlaps with that stay and the activity is plausibly tied to that place, include the location explicitly.
Only propagate a location when the session evidence supports it; otherwise leave the event without a location.

nearby_not_selected.name: Preserve Shared Event Participants
nearby_not_selected.description: When extracting event or relationship memories from messages describing shared activities with first-person plural or reciprocal affirmations, preserve all participants.
content: During extraction, if a message describes an activity with another person using first-person plural (we, us, our, my partner and I), preserve that shared participation in the candidate.
Include the companion and, when stated, their relationship to the speaker; do not rewrite the event as a solo activity.
When a speaker affirms a shared habit or state with a reciprocal phrase ('same here', 'me too', 'likewise'), extract separate candidates for both speaker and addressee when identifiable.
If the co-participant is unknown or 'we' is ambiguous, do not invent a specific person; record only the speaker.
When later messages reveal an omitted participant, use UPDATE or MERGE to add that participant instead of creating a duplicate event.

nearby_not_selected.name: Location Qualifiers for Named Destination Plans
nearby_not_selected.description: When extracting or updating a plan memory that mentions a specific named venue, landmark, or business, include its commonly known location(s) so future location questions can be answered.
content: During extraction, if a plan memory mentions a specific named venue, landmark, or business, add a concise qualifier naming its well-known location(s), e.g., US states or countries.
Use only common knowledge about that entity; do not research or speculate beyond obvious, widely known locations.
If one location is commonly known, record it; if several prominent locations exist, record all commonly known ones, then stop.
Apply the same qualifier when updating an existing plan memory that references the venue.

nearby_not_selected.name: AggregateRepeatedVisitCounts
nearby_not_selected.description: When a message shows a person visiting a place and existing memories record an earlier visit by the same person to the same place, create or update a memory stating the total number of visits.
content: During extraction, when a message states that a person visited a place and another message in the session already establishes an earlier visit by the same person to the same place, generate a candidate memory containing the cumulative number of visits; do not expand this to other places or trips.

During CRUD, when adding or updating a visit event, search the retrieved memory pool for prior visits by the same person to the same place; if found, add a compact visit-count memory or update the existing one so the total count is explicit.
Only aggregate same-person, same-place visits; do not count different locations, do not add a count memory when no prior visit exists, and stop once the count is recorded.
